paper.title_en: Quantum geometry and dynamics of two interacting spins: interplay with entanglement and quantum teleportation
paper.abstract_en: We develop a unified geometric and dynamical description of a two-spin system governed by the isotropic XXX Heisenberg model, incorporating both the antisymmetric Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) interaction and an external magnetic field oriented along the z-axis. Within the Fubini-Study formalism, we derive the quantum metric tensor and show that the system evolves on a compact three-dimensional torus $\mathbb {T}^3$, whose nontrivial topology provides a natural framework for describing the quantum evolution. We further show that, despite its toroidal topology, the associated quantum state manifold remains intrinsically flat. The geometric phase accumulated during the evolution reflects the global properties of the quantum state trajectory in the relevant quantum state space, thereby providing information beyond that contained in the dynamical phase. Entanglement, quantified through Wootters concurrence, is analyzed in connection with the geometric and dynamical properties of the system. By expressing the geometric phase, the Fubini-Study distance, and the evolution speed in terms of concurrence, we find that these quantities arise from the same underlying quantum evolution. In particular, increasing entanglement is accompanied by larger state-space distinguishability and faster quantum evolution, while the DM interaction modifies these behaviors through its influence on the quantum coherences of the spin system. Finally, by examining quantum teleportation through its relation to the geometric phase, the evolution speed, and the Fubini-Study distance, we demonstrate that high teleportation fidelities are associated with larger geometric phases, greater distinguishability between quantum states, and higher evolution speeds. This work provides a coherent framework linking geometry, entanglement, dynamics, and information transfer, highlighting the role of quantum state geometry in understanding quantum information tasks.
